L123:     Abstract
L124:        This document defines an algorithm for generating and verifying a
L125:        succinct non-interactive zero-knowledge argument that for a given
L126:        input x and a circuit C, there exists a witness w, such that C(x,w)
L127:        evaluates to 0.  The technique here combines the MPC-in-the-head
L128:        approach for constructing ZK arguments described in Ligero [ligero]
L129:        with a verifiable computation protocol based on sumcheck for proving
L130:        that C(x,w)=0.
L131:

L246:     1.  Introduction
L247: 
L248:        A zero-knowledge (ZK) scheme allows a Prover who holds an arithmetic
L249:        circuit C defined over a finite field F and two inputs (x,w) to
L250:        convince a Verifier who holds only (C,x) that the Prover knows w such
L251:        that C(x,w) = 0 without revealing any extra information to the
L252:        Verifier.
L253: 
L254:        The concept of a zero-knowledge scheme was introduced by Goldwasser,
L255:        Micali, and Rackoff [GMR], and has since been rigourously explored
L256:        and optimized in the academic literature.
L257: 
L258:        There are several models and efficiency goals that different ZK
L259:        schemes aim to achieve, such as reducing prover time, reducing
L260:        verifier time, or reducing proof size.  Some ZK schemes also impose
L261: 
L262:     Frigo & shelat            Expires 22 April 2027                 [Page 3]
L263:     Internet-Draft                Longfellow ZK                 October 2026
L264:        other requirements to achieve their efficienc goals.  This document
L265:        considers the scenario in which there are no common reference
L266:        strings, or trusted parameter setups that are available to the
L267:        parties.  This immediately rules out several succinct ZK scheme from
L268:        the literature.  In addition, this document also focuses on schemes
L269:        that can be instantiated from a collision-resistant hash function and
L270:        require no other complexity theoretic assumption.  Again, this rules
L271:        out several schemes in the literature.  All of the ZK schemes from
L272:        the literature that remain can be defined in the Interactive Oracle
L273:        Proof (IOP) model, and this document specifies a family of them that
L274:        enjoys both efficiency and simplicity.
L275: 
L276:     1.1.  The Longfellow system
L277: 
L278:        This document specifies the Longfellow ZK scheme described in the
L279:        paper [longfellow].  The scheme is constructed from two components:
L280:        the first is the Ligero scheme, which provides a cryptographic
L281:        commitment scheme that supports an efficient ZK argument system that
L282:        enables proving linear and quadratic constraints on the committed
L283:        witness, and the second is a public-coin interactive protocol (IP)
L284:        for producing an argument that C(x,w)=0 where C is such a circuit, x
L285:        is a public input, and w is a private witness.  The overall scheme
L286:        works by having the Prover commit to the witness w as well as a pad
L287:        used to commit the transcript of the IP, then to run the IP with the
L288:        verifier in a way that produces a commitment to the transcript of the
L289:        IP, and finally, by running the Ligero proof system to prove that the
L290:        transcript in the commitment induces the IP verifier to accept.
L291:        A companion document specifies how the circuit C is specified.
L292: 
L293:     2.  Basic Operations and Notation
L294: 
L295:        The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
L296:        "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this
L297:        document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 6919 [RFC6919].
L298: 
L299:        Except if said otherwise, random choices in this specification refer
L300:        to drawing with uniform distribution from a given set (i.e., "random"
L301:        is short for "uniformly random").  Random choices can be replaced
L302:        with fresh outputs from a cryptographically strong pseudorandom
L303:        generator, according to the requirements in [RFC4086], or
L304:        pseudorandom function.
L305: 
L306:     Frigo & shelat            Expires 22 April 2027                 [Page 4]
L307:     Internet-Draft                Longfellow ZK                 October 2026
L308: 
L309:     2.1.  Array primitives
L310: 
L311:        The notation A[0..N] refers to the array of size N that contains
L312:        A[0],A[1],...,A[N-1], i.e., the right-boundary in the notation X..Y
L313:        is an exclusive index bound.  The following functions are used
L314:        throughout the document:
L315: 
L316:        *  copy(n, Dst, Src): copies n elements from Src to Dst with
L317:           different strides
L318:        *  axpy(n, Y, A, X): sets Y[i] += A*X[i] for 0 <= i < n.
L319:        *  sum(n, A): computes the sum of the first n elements in array A
L320:        *  dot(n, A, Y): computes the dot product of length n between arrays
L321:           A and Y.
L322:        *  add(n, A, Y): returns the array [A[0]+Y[0], A[1]+Y[1], ...,
L323:           A[n-1]+Y[n-1]].
L324:        *  prod(n, A, Y): returns the array [A[0]*Y[0], A[1]*Y[1], ...,
L325:           A[n-1]*Y[n-1]].
L326:        *  equal(n, A, Y): true if A[i]==Y[i] for 0 <= i < n and false
L327:           otherwise.
L328:        *  gather(n, A, I): returns the array [A[I[0]], A[I[1]], ...,
L329:           A[I[n-1]].
L330:        *  A[n][m] = [0]: initializes the 2-dimensional n x m array A to all
L331:           zeroes.
L332:        *  A[0..NREQ] = X : array assignment, this operation copies the first
L333:           NREQ elements of X into the corresponding indicies of the A array.
L334: 
L335:     2.2.  Polynomial operations
L336: 
L337:        This section describes operations on and associated with polynomials
L338:        that are used in the main protocol.
L339: 
L340:     2.2.1.  Extend method in Field F_p
L341: 
L342:        The extend(f, n, m) method interprets the array f[0..n] as the
L343:        evaluations of a polynomial P of degree less than n at the points
L344:        0,...,n-1, and returns the evaluations of the same P at the points
L345:        0,...,m-1.  For sufficiently large fields |F_p| = p >= m, polynomial
L346:        P is uniquely determined by the input, and thus extend is well
L347:        defined.
L348: 
L349:        As there are several algorithms for efficiently performing the extend
L350:        operation, the implementor can choose a suitable one.  In some cases,
L351:        the brute force method of using Lagrange interpolation formulas to
L352:        compute each output point independently may suffice.  One can employ
L353:        a convolution to implement the extend operation, and in some cases,
L354:        either the Number Theoretic Transform or Nussbaumer's algorithm can
L355:        be used to efficiently compute a convolution.
L356: 
L357:     Frigo & shelat            Expires 22 April 2027                 [Page 5]
L358:     Internet-Draft                Longfellow ZK                 October 2026
L359: 
L360:     2.2.2.  Extend method in Field GF 2^k
L361:        The previous section described an extend method that applies to odd
L362:        prime-order finite fields which contain the elements 0,1,2...,m.  In
L363:        the special case of GF(2^k), the extend operator is defined in an
L364:        opinionated way inspired by the Additive FFT algorithm by Lin et al
L365:        [additivefft].  Lin et al. define a novel polynomial basis for
L366:        polynomials as an alternative to the usual monomial basis x^i, and
L367:        give an algorithm for evaluating a degree-(d-1) polynomial at all d
L368:        points in a subspace, for d=2^ell, and for polynomials expressed in
L369:        the novel basis.
L370: 
L371:        Specifically, this document implements GF(2^128) as GF{2}[x] / (Q(x))
L372:        where
L373: 
L374:            Q(x) = x^{128} + x^{7} + x^{2} + x + 1
L375: 
L376:        With this choice of Q(x), x is a generator of the multiplicative
L377:        group of the field.  Next, choose GF(2^16) as the subfield of
L378:        GF(2^128) with g=x^{(2^{128}-1) / (2^{16}-1)} as its generator, and
L379:        beta_i=g^i^ for 0 <= i < 16 as the basis of the subfield.  For
L380:        relevant problem sizes, this allows encoding elements in a commitment
L381:        scheme with 16-bits instead of 128.
L382: 
L383:        Writing j_i for the i-th bit of the binary representation of j, that
L384:        is,
L385:

L393:        In this setting, define the extend operator to interpret the array

L397:        evaluations of the same polynomial p(x) at the injected points
L398:        0,...,m-1.

L407: 
L408:        A ZK protocol may in general instruct the Prover and Verifier to
L409:        engage in multiple rounds of communication.  However, it is often
L410:        more convenient to deploy a non-interactive or single-message
L411:        protocol that only requires a single message from Prover to Verifier.
